newsitem.title: Netherlands: FOCUS-Malaysia touted as Fokker saviour.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia touted as Fokker saviour.

text.p: Malaysia has been touted as a possible 11th hour saviour for bankrupt Dutch plane maker Fokker NV but industry observers are sceptical.
Dutch and Asian newspapers reported on Thursday that the Malaysian government and Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad were involved in last-ditch negotiations to relaunch Fokker.
"We are looking at it. If it is feasible and viable, yes," Mahathir was quoted as saying by Malaysia's Business Times daily in response to reporters' questions.

But in Europe there there was a muted response to the latest scheme to get Fokker back into the air. "I have my grave doubts about it," said Kevin O'Toole, who is business editor of Flight International magazine.
Fokker was declared bankrupt a year ago after majority shareholder Daimler Benz AG of Germany said it would no longer bear Fokker's huge losses.

Court-appointed administrators have kept Fokker's factory near Amsterdam working on a handful of outstanding orders, but unless a miracle happens it will close in a few months and the assets will be liquidated.

The last four planes are due to be delivered between March and May, and Dutch television reported this week that Fokker's final assembly lines were being gradually dismantled as the last few orders edged closer to completion.
In a recent public report the administrators said they were still talking to the chairman of Dutch industrial group Begemann NV, Andre Deleye, about a possible rescue bid.
But they made clear that competing schemes put forward by other interested parties had been rejected as unfeasible.
Begemann officials declined to comment on the group's plans for Fokker and the latest reports of Malaysian involvement.
Stork NV, a Dutch firm which bought some profitable Fokker units last year, confirmed it was taking part in rescue talks at Deleye's invitation but gave no further details.

Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim told reporters that the government had not made any commitment on the Fokker rescue plan in which it would participate through its investment arm, Khazanah Holdings Bhd.
"We are just looking at the proposal and we are negotiating. There is no firm commitment," Anwar was quoted by the New Straits Times daily as saying.
Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant said Begemann's scheme did not envisage the development of a new generation of aircraft, unlike an abortive rescue plan drawn up by South Korea's Samsung Aerospace.

But it said Begemann's own contribution to the project remained shrouded in mystery. "They are not supplying money, technology or, as far as anybody knows management," business reporter Gerard Reijn wrote.
O'Toole of Flight International said that while Malaysia already had modest aircraft maintenance and component production businesses, final assembly was probably still beyond its reach.
"There's a very large gap between being even a large components maker and being capable of final assembly and aircraft design," he said.
"All of the countries of southeast Asia have political ambitions to get into the aerospace market...So far very few of them have succeeded," he added.
